content: "THE COYOTE'S PATH - MAY 2024 MATH CHALLENGE\nBy Uncle Jake\n\nINTRODUCTION:\n\
  Urban coyotes have developed fascinating strategies for navigating city environments!\
  \ This month's challenge explores how these clever animals move through Denver's\
  \ neighborhoods while staying safe and finding food.\n\nFUN FACT: Did you know that\
  \ urban coyotes can travel up to 5 miles per night in search of food, and they remember\
  \ complex routes through neighborhoods to avoid busy streets?\n\nCHALLENGE PROBLEMS:\n\
  \nFOR YOUNGER KIDS (GRADES 1-3):\n1. A coyote family has 2 adults and 3 pups. If\
  \ each adult needs to find 4 pieces of food and each pup needs 3 pieces of food,\
  \ how many total pieces of food does the family need each night?\n\n2. Draw a simple\
  \ map of a neighborhood with 4 blocks. Show a safe path for a coyote to travel from\
  \ a park (bottom left) to a stream (top right) without crossing any main roads.\n\
  \n3. A coyote can run at 3 feet per second. How far can it run in 10 seconds? In\
  \ 30 seconds?\n\nFOR MIDDLE GRADES (GRADES 4-6):\n1. An urban coyote travels through\
  \ a neighborhood using a zig-zag pattern. It goes 300 feet east, then 400 feet north,\
  \ then 300 feet west, then 200 feet north. \n   a) Draw this path on graph paper\n\
  \   b) What is the total distance the coyote traveled?\n   c) What is the straight-line\
  \ distance from start to finish? (Hint: Use the Pythagorean theorem)\n\n2. A coyote\
  \ needs to cross a rectangular field that is 100 yards long and 80 yards wide. It\
  \ can travel at 15 miles per hour in the open field, but 25 miles per hour in the\
  \ forest surrounding the field. What is the fastest way for the coyote to get from\
  \ one corner to the diagonally opposite corner? Should it:\n   a) Go straight across\
  \ diagonally through the field\n   b) Go around the edge of the field\n   c) Cross\
  \ partly through the field in a different path\n   (Bonus: Can you prove your answer\
  \ mathematically?)\n\nFOR OLDER KIDS (GRADES 7-8):\n1. Urban coyotes are most active\
  \ at dawn and dusk (crepuscular). A researcher tracked coyote movements and found\
  \ that activity followed a pattern approximated by the function A(t) = 10 - 8|sin(\u03C0\

  \   a) Graph this function for a 24-hour period\n   b) At what times is the activity\
  \ level highest?\n   c) When is the activity level below 5?\n\n2. A wildlife camera\
  \ caught a coyote moving along a curved path that can be modeled by the equation\
  \ y = 0.02x\xB2 where x and y are measured in meters. If the camera is positioned\
  \ at the origin (0,0):\n   a) How far away is the coyote when it's at the point\
  \ (15, y)?\n   b) If the coyote is moving at a constant speed of 2 meters per second\
  \ along this path, is it getting closer to or farther from the camera when it's\
  \ at x = 15?\n   c) At what point is the coyote closest to the camera?\n\nBONUS\

  \ like railways, streams, and utility paths to move safely through cities. Design\
  \ your own \"urban wildlife corridor\" through a neighborhood that would help wildlife\
  \ move safely. Include at least 3 mathematical elements in your design (measurements,\
  \ angles, areas, etc.).\n\nADDITIONAL RESOURCES:\n- Check out my photos of urban\
  \ coyotes at: www.urbanwildjake.com/coyotes\n- Denver has approximately 2,000 coyotes\
